messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Salesperson
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The flood came at night, while Derek was asleep in his first-floor apartment in the small Missouri town where he’d grown up. He woke to water already lapping at the edge of his mattress, the sound of it rushing under the door, the terrible groan of the building shifting. He scrambled onto his dresser, then through the window into the black water, grabbing a tree branch that kept him from being swept away. For hours he clung there, listening to people scream, watching cars and debris surge past in the dark. He was certain he would die. When rescue came at dawn, he was hypothermic and shaking, but alive. What stayed with him, though, was not just the terror of that night—it was the way the world had turned, in an instant, into something that wanted to kill him.

In the months afterward, Derek tried to go back to his life. He worked as a salesperson at a regional auto dealership, a job that required him to drive to client meetings across three counties. But he found himself avoiding routes that passed near rivers, creeks, or even large drainage ditches. Rainy days became unbearable. The first time a spring thunderstorm rolled in, he pulled his car over on the highway, hands locked on the wheel, heart hammering, certain he could hear water rising even though the road was dry. He had come to believe that any stretch of low ground, any patch of woods that looked like the ones that had lined the flooded streets, could trigger the same helplessness. What frightened him most was that he didn’t always see the flood in his mind when it happened. Sometimes he would just feel the terror—the cold, the panic, the certainty of drowning—without any image at all, as though his body remembered what his mind could not.

There were parts of that night he could not retrieve no matter how hard he tried. He knew he had been in the water for hours, but the sequence was gone. He remembered the tree branch, the screams, the gray light of dawn—but there were gaps, whole stretches of time that felt erased. And when he did remember, the terror came back undiminished, as fresh as if he were still clinging to that branch. These memories, or the absence of them, made him feel like a stranger to himself. He used to be someone who could handle things, who knew who he was. Now he felt hollow, untethered, as though the person he had been had drowned in that flood and left only this anxious, watchful shell behind. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. His job was just motion. His relationships, never deep, had become almost nonexistent. He had stopped returning calls from friends because he couldn’t explain why he spent his evenings pacing his new second-floor apartment, checking the locks, listening for the sound of water.

The world had become a landscape of threats. Every low-lying road, every overcast sky, every moment of vulnerability felt like the beginning of another disaster. He woke at night to check whether he was safe, though he knew logically that his apartment was on a hill. He was hypervigilant during the day, scanning the horizon for storm clouds, monitoring the ground beneath his feet for any hint of dampness. This constant watchfulness only deepened his belief that he could not rely on other people—they hadn't been there in the water, they didn't understand the danger that still lurked everywhere, and they couldn't protect him. He had learned that safety was something he had to enforce himself, and he was failing.

The cycle tightened over the course of a year. A trigger—a drive past a creek swollen by rain—would bring the memory rushing back, and with it the appalling realization that he was not the person he used to be. That sense of lost identity would sharpen his vigilance, and his vigilance would confirm that the world was unsafe, which reinforced his feeling that nothing mattered anymore. And then the vigilance itself would lead him to notice more triggers: a patch of moss on a curb, the smell of wet earth, the sound of a storm drain gurgling. Each new trigger pulled him back into the memory, and the memory reminded him of who he had become. He had stopped going on sales calls that required crossing bridges. His manager had noticed. His commissions had dropped. He was running out of excuses.

What finally brought Derek to seek help was not the fear, but the exhaustion. He was tired of being on guard, tired of the way his own mind ambushed him with feelings he couldn't name, tired of the hollow, meaningless days. He sat in the therapist's office with his hands clasped, and said, quietly, that he just wanted to feel like himself again—though he wasn't sure that person even existed anymore.
